doc.title: Skitch Henderson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Milford, Connecticut, October 31, 1998

title: Starting to conduct and the click track
summary: Conducting began by standing up to give time; Victor Young urged lessons; how click tracks worked.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: You had your turn under the gun eventually on the podium.

Yeah, well I’ll tell you, you know how I started? The conductor wouldn’t show up. It was always in a panic. Often the conductor was the orchestrator or composer or arranger, dishwasher, and may times they’d be late on the date. So you know everybody’d be looking at their watch at whatever the call was, so they’d say, “Kid why don’t you stand up” — because as a piano, I never had, maybe a belltone or something. “Kid, why don’t you stand up and give us some time.” That’s really how I started.

Time. And then Victor Young said there was a wonderful gentlemen by the name of Albert Coates who was a conductor in the period of Thomas Beecham in England, and he was driven out of England by Beecham with his wealth. And he formed an orchestra for the Czar before the royal family in Russia was done away with. And there are still records with him, Coates, and he was a great, great conductor. And Victor Young said, “If you had any brains you’d go take some conducting lessons right now. Maybe you won’t learn anything but just do it.” And that’s really how, then I began to see how serious it was and how tough it was. Because most of the guys in Hollywood were leaders, you know we called leaders. You know they’d drop their arm and hope you’d play, because everything ran from the click track, so the musicians were built-in, you could leave them alone they probably could play the cue better than anybody else.
Those clicks, did they work on the quarter note? Were you hearing the quarter note or were your hearing something different?

No you’d generally hear a time factor leading to like if it was, let’s say you had a [scats] you’d hear maybe three clicks ahead of it [scats] and you’d go [scats]. It would be set up ahead of time. It was a conducting cue is really what it was. It would drive you crazy. At the end of the day you hated everything.
